Varun, you say Ishan “deserved” that push because he kept boasting. Let me, your Nazia Nani, tell you something I did.
When I was eleven in Lucknow, a girl called Rehana sat next to me. She always corrected my spellings, loudly, in front of the class. One day, in the courtyard, I pushed her into the puddle by the hand-pump. Her uniform was soaked.
When the headmistress called me, I said, “She's such a know-all. She was asking for it.” I truly believed it. Rehana was the problem, not my hands.
Then my own Abba said, very quietly, “Did Rehana push you, Nazia?” I had no answer.
I went to her house that evening with my own dry dupatta to lend her. She took it. We stayed friends for sixty years.

qa.q: Where did young Nazia push Rehana?
qa.a: She pushed her into the puddle by the hand-pump in the courtyard.

qa.q: Why did young Nazia truly believe Rehana was asking for it?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and angry at being corrected in front of the class, so blaming Rehana let her feel her push was justified.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Nazia make the choice that changed things?
qa.a: After her Abba's quiet question, she chose to go to Rehana's house that evening with a dry dupatta to make amends.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt standing in her soaked uniform?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt shocked and embarrassed, and hurt that Nazia called it her fault.

grounding: The grandmother's memory shows a child blaming the classmate she pushed for being annoying, until a question returns the responsibility.

passage:
The school bus was stuck in rain traffic near the flyover, windows fogged, forty children packed in and the conductor shouting over the thunder.
Tenzin, behind Kamal, kept kicking the back of his seat. Tap, tap, tap. Kamal turned twice. “Stop it.”
The third time, Kamal stood and shoved Tenzin hard. Tenzin's head bumped the window frame and his eyes filled.
The conductor pulled them apart. “Why?”
“He was so annoying! He kept kicking. He deserved it,” Kamal said, breathing fast. Everyone was hot and sticky and cross; it felt obvious to him.
The conductor held Tenzin's head gently, checking the bump. “Kicking a seat is wrong,” the conductor said. “Pushing a head into glass is a different kind of wrong. That one's yours.”
Kamal sat down, still angry, but his hands were trembling now.

qa.q: What did Tenzin keep doing on the bus?
qa.a: Tenzin kept kicking the back of Kamal's seat, tap, tap, tap.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel sure Tenzin deserved the push?
qa.a: Kamal was hot, cross and angry, so Tenzin's kicking felt like the whole cause, making his own push feel justified.

qa.q: What could Kamal do differently on a crowded, rainy ride next time?
qa.a: He could ask the conductor to move him or deal with the kicking, instead of pushing.

qa.q: How did the conductor see the push differently from Kamal?
qa.a: The conductor saw two separate wrongs and held Kamal responsible for the push, not Tenzin.

grounding: The passage shows a child on a cramped rainy bus justifying a push by saying the annoying classmate deserved it.

Coach's note, under-15 football, Tuesday practice.
During the water break I heard two older boys call Thomas “Fatty Tom” again and toss his bottle into the bushes. Thomas went to get it without saying anything. His ears were red.
Sangeeta, who is his closest friend on the team, was standing right there. When he came back she said, “Thomas, you really need to stop being so touchy. They're just messing around. Toughen up.” Then she jogged off quickly, as if to end the conversation.
She looked uncomfortable, not unkind. I think it was easier for her to fix Thomas than to face the two older boys.
After practice I spoke to the two boys, told them the name-calling stops now, and informed the head of sports and both sets of parents by phone that evening. I also checked in with Thomas, who said it happens most days. I will talk to Sangeeta tomorrow about what a friend can do.

qa.a: They tossed his bottle into the bushes during the water break.

qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable and anxious about confronting the older boys, so telling Thomas to change felt easier and less scary.

qa.q: How could an adult help Sangeeta be a better friend in this situation?
qa.a: The coach could talk with her about standing next to Thomas, saying “that's not okay”, and telling an adult, instead of asking him to toughen up.

qa.q: What is it like for Thomas to hear his closest friend say he is too touchy?
qa.a: Thomas likely feels hurt and alone, because even the friend who saw it treats the bullying as his problem.

grounding: The coach's note shows a teenager who sees her friend bullied telling him to toughen up, avoiding discomfort by making the target responsible.

Thursday night.
They did it again at recess. Called Kamal “Kamala” and did the high voice. Someone flicked his ear. Kamal just sat there doing his maths.
After, I said, “Bro, you need to stop reacting. Just laugh along. You're too sensitive.” He looked at me like I'd slapped him.
Writing this now I feel sick. He didn't react. He sat there. I said it because I didn't want to be the one who tells them to stop. It's easier if Kamal is the problem.
So at 5 I went back to school and told Mr Pillai, our class teacher. He listened properly, asked for names, and called Kamal's mother while I was still there. He said he'll speak to the boys first thing tomorrow and that I did the right thing telling him.
Tomorrow I'm sitting with Kamal at recess. Not saying anything clever. Just sitting.
— Vaibhav

passage:
Ganga sat on her suitcase outside the Andheri building. The flat she had paid a deposit for, through a listing with lovely photos, did not exist. The “owner” had stopped answering.
Her brother Eshaan arrived from work, read the chat and exploded. “Ganga! You sent money to a stranger without seeing the place? How could you be so dumb? Everyone knows these scams.”
Ganga stared at the ground. Her face burned. She had checked the photos, the address, even the owner's voice. Now she just felt stupid.
Eshaan stopped. He saw her hands shaking. He sat down on the pavement next to her.
“Sorry. That was the wrong thing to say. They're professionals at this. Tell me everything, from the start.”
She told him. Then together they called the bank's helpline and filed a complaint on the cyber-crime portal before 8 p.m.

qa.q: What turned out not to exist?
qa.a: The flat she had paid a deposit for, through a listing with lovely photos, did not exist.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel after Eshaan called her dumb?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and stupid, staring at the ground with her face burning, even though she had checked carefully.

qa.q: Which of Eshaan's responses helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting down, apologising, listening to the whole story and then calling the bank and filing a complaint; it eased her shame and gave practical next steps.

qa.q: Why might Eshaan have exploded at first?
qa.a: He was probably shocked and frightened for his sister, and anger at her felt easier than facing that anyone can be tricked.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman cheated by a rental scam being blamed for not being smarter, then helped by listening and practical steps.

When I told my roommate Kalyani, she said, “Seriously, Jasleen? That's the oldest trick. Didn't you read the warning email?” I laughed with her, and then cried in the shower.
For two days I told nobody else. I felt like the stupidest person on campus.
What helped was the student welfare officer. I went in expecting a lecture. Instead they said, “They had your details. You were targeted, not careless.” They helped me file a complaint and write to the bank that afternoon.
Later Kalyani apologised. She said she'd been scared it could happen to her.

passage:
Subject: What I should have said

Mehak,

On Friday, when you told me the new manager had been calling you into his cabin late and making comments about your clothes, the first thing I said was, “Why did you keep going in alone?”

I've replayed that all weekend. It was the wrong question. It put the whole thing on you.

The right questions are: who made the comments? Who chose to call a junior into a cabin after hours? Who has the power to stop it? Those answers all point to him, not to you.

I'm sorry. You trusted me with this and I made you defend yourself.

If you want, I'll come with you to the internal committee on Monday, or sit with you while you write it down first. Whatever you decide, I'm on your side.

Arnab

So, you asked what changed how I talk to my team. It was one Tuesday, honestly.
I'm Jatin, I lead a small design team. Zeenat, one of our juniors, came to me upset. A senior from another team had presented her whole layout at the client meeting as his own. And the first thing out of my mouth was, “Why didn't you put your name on the file?”
She went quiet. I saw her shoulders drop. And I heard myself. I'd made her the one who had to explain.
So I stopped and said, “Sorry. Wrong question. Who presented it? Who knew it was yours and chose not to say?”
We went through it: he'd seen her drafts, he'd been told they were hers. That was a choice, and it was his.
I took it to his manager that afternoon, with her files. Now, whenever something goes wrong, I ask who acted first, before I ask who should have stopped them.

qa.a: Jatin felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, noticing it made Zeenat the one who had to explain.

I remember the night I paid for the essay better than most things from third year.
I, Shalini, had a family wedding, two internals and a psychology report due on Monday. A girl on the hostel group said she “helped” with reports. I told myself: there are coaching centres selling full degree certificates in this city. Compared with that, one report was nothing.
I sent the money. I got a clean, polished file. It had my name on top.
And I couldn't submit it. My friend Pallavi found me staring at it at 2 a.m. She didn't lecture. She said, “Does this look like something you'd be proud of in five years?”
I deleted the file and wrote to my professor asking for two extra days. She gave them.
My own report was worse. It was also mine.

Nandini,

Silly, maybe. But it's the first time I've noticed how easily “others do worse” pulls me along.

Deepika

Monday: Deepika knocked over the ink bottle on her brother Gautam's drawing. When Amma came running, Deepika said, “Mitthu jumped on the table.” The cat was asleep on the window. Amma didn't see.
Wednesday: Gautam was still sulking. Deepika told Nani the story: Mitthu jumped, knocked the bottle, ran off. She added that Mitthu's tail swished it. Nani nodded.
Saturday: At dinner, Gautam grumbled about his drawing again. Deepika said, sure as anything, “It was Mitthu! I saw his paws in the ink.”
Then she stopped. Had there been paw prints? She tried to picture them. She could picture them. But she could also picture her own elbow, and the bottle tipping.
Her tummy went funny. She wasn't sure anymore which picture was real.

Seema, you're saying your friend now really believes her own story about the missing eraser. Let me, your Rukmini Paati, tell you: I've done that.
When I was eight, in Madurai, I broke my mother's glass bangle while trying it on. When she found the pieces, I said, “The monkey came in from the terrace.” Monkeys did come, so everyone believed it.
I told that monkey story at every family function. I added details. The monkey's scratched ear, the way it grabbed the drawer.
Forty years later, my sister laughed and said, “There was no monkey, Rukku. I saw you drop it.”
I was so shocked. I could see that monkey in my mind, clear as you are now. That's when I learned how a story told many times starts to feel like memory.

qa.q: Why was Rukmini so shocked forty years later?
qa.a: She had told the monkey story so often that it felt like a true memory, so she was stunned and confused to learn she made it up.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Rukmini have stopped the fib from growing?
qa.a: When her mother found the pieces, or at the first family function, she could have told the truth before adding details.

qa.q: How might Rukmini's sister have felt keeping that secret for forty years?
qa.a: The sister might have felt amused, maybe a little uneasy, knowing the truth while everyone laughed at the monkey story.

grounding: The grandmother's memory shows a childhood fib, retold many times, becoming something she truly remembered.

“Physics test tomorrow. You ready?” Amandeep asked, packing her bag.
“Totally,” Swati said. “I read through all the notes twice. It all looks familiar.”
“Did you try the numericals?”
“No need. I remember the formulas. I've seen them a hundred times.”
“Okay. Can you explain why the ball falls at the same rate as the feather in a vacuum?”
“Uh. Because… gravity is the same.” Swati waved her hand. “I know it. I just can't say it right now.”
Three days later, Amandeep found her by the notice board.
“Thirty-eight out of eighty?” Swati whispered. “I was so sure. The questions looked like the notes, and then I couldn't do any of them.”
“Reading isn't the same as doing,” Amandeep said gently. “Want to try the numericals together for the next one?”
Swati nodded, still stunned.

The morning of the history exam, I felt calm. Almost smug.
I had gone through the textbook twice, highlighter in hand. My friend Sonali asked if I wanted to quiz each other. I said no, I already knew it. The chapter on the Mughal land revenue system looked so familiar I could have drawn the page.

Tutor's note, Saturday batch, Class 10 maths.
Gurleen came in this week confident. She told me she had “gone over” quadratics three times and felt sure. I asked her to solve one problem on the board. She wrote the formula perfectly, then stopped at the second step and said, “I know this, I just need to see it.”
In Thursday's school test she scored 12 out of 40. Today she was very quiet and kept saying, “But I read it all.”
Her study partner Tushar said they had mostly read through solved examples together, not tried any alone.
What I did next: we closed all books and worked three problems from scratch, slowly. She got the third one right. I suggested she try one blank problem each night and mark only what she can do without looking. I'll check in with her next Saturday and send a short note to her parents so they know the plan.

qa.q: What did Gurleen score in Thursday's school test?
qa.a: She scored 12 out of 40.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen keep saying “But I read it all”?
qa.a: She felt shocked and confused, because reading the chapter three times had made her feel sure she understood it.

qa.q: What plan did the tutor suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Solving one blank problem each night without looking, which tests real understanding instead of familiarity.

qa.q: How might Tushar see their study sessions now?
qa.a: Tushar may realise that reading solved examples together felt productive but left them both unprepared, and feel uneasy about how ready Tushar really was.

grounding: The tutor's note shows a teenager who skimmed notes feeling ready, then being surprised by the result because familiarity was mistaken for understanding.
